The shipment record confirms the consignment's actual and chargeable weight is exactly 50.0 kg (no minimum-weight floor applies since 50 kg already exceeds the 25 kg floor per §1). Under §2, the two rate bands are written as "under 50 kg" (₹9.50/kg) and "over 50 kg" (₹8.25/kg) — both strict inequalities relative to 50 kg. A consignment weighing exactly 50 kg therefore falls into neither stated band, and no per-kg rate is written in the contract for this exact weight. This is not a case where one reading is merely inconvenient; it is a literal gap in the text, which the rate card's own ambiguities list independently corroborates. Neither the shipment facts nor any other clause (service level, special handling, etc.) supplies a tiebreaker — service level is standard with no special handling, so nothing else in the contract bears on which band should apply. Because the correct per-kg rate cannot be determined from the contract as written, and picking either band would mean inventing a rate the contract doesn't actually state, this must go to a human for a ruling (or a negotiated fix with the carrier) rather than being resolved by inference.

The shipment record shows 260 kg billed weight and 800 km distance, placing this consignment in the §1 'up to and including 500 kg' band at ₹18.00/km, yielding base freight of 14400. The express service premium of 15% (§2) correctly applies given service_level is 'express', adding 2160 on the base. The fuel surcharge of 12% (§3) then applies to the combined base-plus-express figure, per its stated compounding basis. No special_handling values are present on the shipment record, so the §4 residential accessorial (whitelisted as the only payable accessorial under §5) does not fire, and no other accessorial is contractually payable. Recomputing the trace step by step against the verbatim contract text confirms the expected amount is correctly derived and the billed amount includes an unexplained excess with no clause supporting it.

The shipment record shows a standard-service consignment of 700 kg over 800 km with no special handling. Applying the contract: base freight falls in the 501–2,000 kg band at the per-km rate specified in §1, the express premium in §2 correctly does not fire since service_level is "standard" (not express), and the 12% fuel surcharge in §3 is applied on the base freight as required. This fully accounts for the expected amount in the pricing trace. The billed amount exceeds this by a fixed sum that cannot be explained by any contract mechanism: there is no special handling triggering the residential accessorial (§4), and §5 explicitly states no other accessorial charges are payable under this agreement absent a prior written rate confirmation, none of which is evidenced here. The extra amount therefore appears to be an unauthorized or uncontracted charge.

Consignment FF-8003 corresponds to a single shipment, SH-4003 (Pune to Kolhapur, delivered once on 2026-07-06), yet it was billed in full on two separate Falcon invoices (07A and 07B), each at the same amount and each individually matching the contract-computed expected charge for that one shipment under §1's per-km, weight-banded base freight (plus applicable premiums/surcharges). The shipment record shows no second movement, no re-delivery, and no split shipment that would justify a second charge, and nothing in the evidence (no credit note, no correction reference under §8) explains a legitimate second occurrence. Since the contract's freight charge is for carriage actually rendered on a given consignment, and only one carriage occurred, the second billing of the same consignment has no contractual basis and represents a duplicate charge that should not be paid twice.

The pricing trace correctly applies §1: a weight component (billed weight × ₹6/kg) plus a distance component (distance_km × ₹2/km), summing to the contract-governed freight charge. The shipment record confirms standard service level and no special_handling entries, so the cold chain premium in §3 correctly does not fire (there is no cold_chain flag on this shipment), and no other surcharge or accessorial applies under this contract. The billed amount exceeds this contract-derived figure by the delta shown in the evidence, with nothing in the shipment facts, service level, or special handling that would justify the difference. The only ambiguity noted on this rate card concerns whether 'booked lane distance' in §1 could differ from a shipment's recorded distance_km, but no evidence here (shipment record or invoice) supplies an alternative booked-lane distance value that would reconcile the billed figure with the contract formula, so this ambiguity does not bear on the specific overcharge shown. This is a determinable contractual overcharge under §1.

invoice_findings.description: invoice qualifies for 'Volume incentive discount' under every computable date basis (40 consignments, threshold gt 12), but the carrier's declared discount is 0.0
invoice_findings.justification: All three candidate counting bases (by invoice document, by booking-date calendar month, and by ship-date calendar month) agree that ALPINE-0726 tendered 40 consignments in the relevant month, well above the >12 threshold in §5, so entitlement to the 5% volume incentive discount is not in question — the carrier's declared discount of 0 is inconsistent with the contract. However, the exact rupee shortfall cannot yet be computed: the discount applies to the invoice total, and one line on this same invoice is not yet pricing-determined, so the invoice total itself is incomplete. Because a concrete, actionable figure isn't available, this must be escalated rather than disputed outright — once the pending line is resolved and the invoice total is finalized, the 5% shortfall can be computed and pursued.
